categories.description: Semantics, forms, media, accessibility, and document structure.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.summary: Learn why semantic tags improve accessibility, SEO, and maintainability.

sections.heading: Why semantics matter
sections.content: Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags (like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <footer>) instead of generic ones. This helps screen readers, search engines, and developers understand the page structure.

sections.heading: Common semantic tags
sections.content: Use <header> for introductory content, <nav> for navigation, <main> for primary content, <section> for thematic grouping, <article> for self-contained composition, and <footer> for closing information.

sections.heading: Accessibility checklist
sections.content: Prefer headings in order, label form controls, ensure interactive elements are keyboard accessible, and avoid using only color to convey meaning.

lessons.title: Forms & Validation
lessons.summary: Build forms that are usable: labels, input types, constraints, and error states.

sections.heading: Always label inputs
sections.content: Use <label for=...> to connect labels with inputs. This improves usability and screen reader experience.

sections.heading: Use native validation
sections.content: Leverage HTML attributes like required, min/max, pattern, type, and inputmode. Provide helpful error messages.

sections.heading: Progressive enhancement
sections.content: Rely on HTML validation and basic behavior first. Add richer UX with JavaScript (optional) without breaking core functionality.

categories.title: CSS

lessons.title: The CSS Box Model
lessons.summary: Understand content, padding, borders, margins, and sizing behaviors.

sections.heading: Components
sections.content: Every element’s rendered size is determined by content box, padding, border, and margin. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes border and padding.

sections.heading: Margin collapsing
sections.content: Vertical margins can collapse between block elements in specific situations. This affects layout spacing unexpectedly if you’re not aware.

sections.heading: Practical guidance
sections.content: Prefer consistent box-sizing (commonly border-box) and use spacing utilities/patterns to avoid “magic numbers”.

lessons.title: Flexbox Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Learn flex containers, main/cross axes, and how to align items.

sections.heading: Container vs items
sections.content: Set display: flex on the container. Flex children become flex items. Properties on the container control the axes and wrapping.

sections.heading: Key properties
sections.content: justify-content aligns along the main axis. align-items aligns along the cross axis. gap controls spacing between items.

sections.heading: When to use flex
sections.content: Flexbox is great for one-dimensional layouts (row OR column). For two-dimensional layouts, consider CSS Grid.

lessons.title: Scope & Closures
lessons.summary: Closures are functions that remember variables from their lexical scope.

sections.heading: Lexical scope
sections.content: A variable’s scope is determined by where it’s declared in the source code. Inner functions can access outer variables.

sections.heading: What is a closure?
sections.content: When an inner function uses variables from an outer function, it “closes over” those variables. That’s the closure.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.content: Closures enable patterns like data encapsulation, callbacks, and function factories.

lessons.title: Async/Await Basics
lessons.summary: Write asynchronous code that looks synchronous using async/await.

sections.heading: async functions
sections.content: An async function always returns a Promise. Use await to pause within the async function until the Promise resolves.

sections.heading: Error handling
sections.content: Use try/catch around await calls. Rejections are caught like thrown errors.
